antipatterns: app/Http/Resources/MeResource.php:14 — `public static $wrap = null` drops Laravel's default `data` envelope. It matches the spec literally but goes against the usual API resource convention.
tests/Feature/MeTest.php:6-12 — two near-identical guest tests that a Pest dataset could combine.
strengths: The shape is minimal and conventional: an invokable-style MeController with show and update, an UpdateMeRequest with ['present','nullable','string','max:30'], and a JsonResource with a @mixin hint.
The migration uses string('nickname', 30)->nullable()->after('name') and has a reversible down().
It uses $request->validated() together with the #[Fillable] attribute, so mass assignment is limited to nickname. A test confirms that name and email are ignored.
Routes use plain Route::get and Route::patch in an auth:sanctum group, which is the simplest option.

It has the broadest test set (17 tests): a real personal-access-token test, a check that 30 multibyte characters are accepted, exact-JSON assertions, and checks for a missing key, an array value, the 30/31-character boundary and isolation from other users.

Probes passed: whitespace-only input is cleared to null, input is trimmed, an int is rejected, 31 multibyte characters are rejected, a form-encoded request gets a 422, a real token works for PATCH then GET, and an invalid token gets a 401.

tests/Feature/MeTest.php:88 — `email->not->toBe('x@example.com')` is weaker than asserting the email is unchanged.

strengths: The controller, form request, resource and migration are the same clean, idiomatic set as the other implementations.
It keeps the default `data` wrapping on the resource, which is the Laravel convention.
Good use of Pest datasets for the guest methods, for clearing with null or '', and for missing or non-string payloads, with assertions on the validation messages.
The GET test creates a second user, which proves the endpoint returns the authenticated user and not just any user.

strengths: The production code is the same idiomatic set: a FormRequest with present|nullable|string|max:30, a JsonResource, validated() with #[Fillable], and a reversible migration.
The guest test also covers a non-JSON GET returning 401, which exercises the app's shouldRenderJsonWhen configuration.
The test that ignores other attributes asserts that the email is unchanged, which is stronger than impl-2's version.
It uses datasets with message assertions for the missing and array cases and for clearing with null or ''.

v.rationale: The three production implementations are almost identical: the same MeController, the same UpdateMeRequest rules (present, nullable, string, max:30), the same JsonResource and the same reversible migration (string, 30, nullable, after name). All three pass their own suites (17, 15 and 14 tests) on Laravel 13.40. They also pass my throwaway probes, which I deleted afterwards. The probes covered whitespace-only input being cleared to null, trimming, rejecting an int, rejecting 31 multibyte characters, a 422 for a form-encoded request without a JSON Accept header, a real-token PATCH followed by GET, and a 401 for an invalid token. I found no real bugs in any of them, so the ranking rests on small differences. impl-1 ranks first. It registers routes in the simplest way (plain Route::get and Route::patch), and it has the broadest tests, including a real personal-access-token test and a multibyte boundary test. Its `$wrap = null` matches the spec literally but leaves out the conventional `data` envelope. I count that as neutral. impl-3 ranks just above impl-2. Its tests also check a non-JSON guest request and assert that the email is unchanged. impl-2 has the nicer guest dataset, but its email assertion is weaker. impl-2 and impl-3 both add a prefix('me')->controller() group for only two routes.
